newsitem.title: USA: High stakes game in Washington over gambling panel.
newsitem.headline: High stakes game in Washington over gambling panel.

text.p: A high-stakes game is being played in Washington over who should be named to a new national commission on gambling, with each side accusing the other of trying to stack the deck.

In recent years casino gambling has become a major U.S. industry -- about half as big as the soft drinks industry -- and those who are trying to stop its spread fear the new commission will be tilted in favour of gambling advocates.

"When these commissioners are finally appointed, we'll see whether Las Vegas turns their millions in (political) contributions into a political jackpot," said Tom Grey, executive director of the National Coalition Against Legalised Gambling, a grassroots organisation.

The coalition says the gambling industry gave more than $4.4 million in political contributions to both national parties in 1995-96 and 10 people connected to gaming interests have attended coffees at the White House since early 1996.
Grey said Steve Wynn, chairman of a Las Vegas casino company, had played golf with President Clinton last May.

"The president may know how to run the government, but I know how to fight gambling. I can tell you, when Steve Wynn wants to play golf with you, it's not because you are a good golf partner," Grey said.

But lobbyists for gaming interests scoff at the idea that they could influence appointments to the gambling study commission, especially by Clinton, a Democrat who has yet to announce his three choices for the panel.

Frank Fahrenkopf, president of the American Gaming Association, noted he had been Republican party national chairman from 1983 to 1989. "I can assure you the White House doesn't call Frank Fahrenkopf every day," he said.

Gambling opponents say a tidal wave of legalised gambling has swept across the United States since the late 1980s, and at their urging Congress last July passed a bill to establish the commission to study the industry's impact on society. It will have nine members, three appointed by the president and three each by House and Senate leaders, and is supposed to complete its report within two years.
Casinos have been legalised in 21 more states since 1988. Last year, the casino gaming industry reported $25 billion in total revenues, double those in 1990.

Those who pushed hard for the commission want it to study the relationship between gambling and crime, corruption, and what they call the "cannibalization" of other businesses by the industry. But two of the six people already named to the panel by congressional leaders have links to the industry.

House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, named Terri Lanni, chairman of the MGM Grand casino in Las Vegas, and House Democratic leader Richard Gephardt of Missouri named John Wilhelm, a union official who has represented workers whose livelihoods depend on the gambling industry.
"The gambling people first tried to kill the commission, then gut it, now they are trying to stack it," Grey charged.

But Fahrenkopf countered that there was at least one known gambling opponent among those who have been appointed -- James Dobson, president of a group called "Focus on the Family" in Colorado Springs, who was appointed by Senate Republican leader Trent Lott of Mississippi.
Fahrenkopf noted Gingrich also appointed Kay James, a dean at Pat Robertson's Regent University in Virginia Beach. Robertson's Christian Coalition opposes gambling.
Fahrenkopf charged gambling opponents "have got their people on the commission early and now they want to pull up the gate."
The other two people who have been apppointed -- Paul Moore, a radiologist from Pascagoula, Miss., and Leo McCarthy, former lieutenant governor of California -- are thought to be neutral on gambling.
So attention is focused on the White House, which was expected to announce its picks this week but has not done so yet after some of the candidates' names appeared in the press.

The Las Vegas Sun said a possible choice was Bill Bible, chairman of the Nevada Gaming Control Board, which regulates gambling in the state. The Washington Post said the short list included Tadd Johnson, a member of an Indian tribe with a casino in Minnesota, and former New Jersey state treasurer Richard Leone, a critic of gambling.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry declined Monday to say when Clinton would announce his picks, saying only that he would do it "when he's confident that he's got the right and most superbly qualified nominees for the commission."
